To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the thermal Goldstone boson modes are not the same as the zero mass Goldstone modes.
the unmasked thermal Goldstone modes are not only massless but also noninteracting, i.e. the thermal correlation functions are given in terms of free thermal propagators.
the thermal Goldstone boson can be identified with a zero-mass particle and the corresponding contribution is a specific term in the decomposition of thermal correlation function.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the dynamics of a system of interacting bosons in a thermal environment.
the study of the thermal properties of a system of particles with a non-trivial spectrum.
the problem of extracting the zero modes of Goldstone particles from a thermal bath, which has been the object of much recent discussion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no thermal Goldstone boson in the sense of a particle with zero mass.
the Goldstone boson is not a particle of zero rest mass but a particle of zero energy.
the Goldstone bosons are not thermalized.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the thermal modes of a zero-mass particle are unmasked in the decomposition.

the thermal correlation functions contain a contribution which is a direct consequence of the spontaneous breakdown of an external symmetry and which can be attributed, in an appropriate way, to a particle of a mass which is zero at zero temperature and which increases as the temperature rises.
the Goldstone modes of a thermal system can be unambiguously identified as a specific set of modes of a zero-mass particle.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the modes of Goldstones are not thermalized in the usual sense, and their contribution to the thermal correlation functions is of a nonthermal nature.
these contributions are not thermal Goldstone boson excitations.
the thermal mass of a Goldstone boson can be extracted from the imaginary part of a two-point function in the limit of small momentum.
